sections.text: BMI, BMR and TDEE answer three different questions. BMI says how your weight compares with your height. BMR is an estimate of the calories your body uses at complete rest. TDEE is BMR multiplied by an activity factor, which gives an estimate of the calories you use on a typical day. BMI does not feed into the BMR or TDEE formulas, but the three numbers are linked because weight appears in all of them. This article follows one person through all three so you can see how a change in weight changes the others.
What each number is, in one line

rows: Where does my weight sit for my height?
What does my body use at rest?
Weight, height, age, sex (or lean mass)
What do I use on a typical day?

sections.text: BMI is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. Our BMR and TDEE calculators default to the Mifflin-St Jeor equation: 10 x weight (kg) + 6.25 x height (cm) - 5 x age + 5 for men, or - 161 for women. TDEE multiplies that by 1.2 (sedentary), 1.375 (light exercise 1 to 2 days a week), 1.55 (moderate, 3 to 5 days), 1.725 (heavy, 6 to 7 days) or 1.9 (athlete or very physical job).
Worked example: one person, three numbers
Assumptions: a 35-year-old woman, 165 cm tall, 82 kg (about 181 lb), light exercise one or two days a week. All figures are hypothetical and rounded to the nearest whole number or one decimal.

items: BMI = 82 / 1.65 squared = 82 / 2.7225 = 30.1. That is in the CDC obesity range (30 or above), class 1.
The weight range for BMI 18.5 to 24.9 at 165 cm is 50.4 to 67.8 kg (about 111 to 149 lb).
TDEE at the light-exercise factor = 1,515 x 1.375 = 2,083 kcal/day.

sections.text: The BMI step tells her which category she is in and what a BMI-based weight range looks like. The BMR and TDEE steps give a maintenance estimate. Neither step is a diagnosis or a prescription.
How the numbers move as weight changes

Because weight is an input to the BMR equation, BMR and TDEE fall as weight falls. In the Mifflin-St Jeor equation each kilogram changes BMR by 10 kcal/day. The table recalculates the same woman at lower weights, with age, height and the 1.375 factor held constant.

From 82 kg to 67.8 kg, her maintenance estimate drops by about 195 kcal/day (2,083 to 1,888). That is the reason a calorie target set at the start of a weight change goes out of date. Recalculate when your weight has changed noticeably rather than keeping the original number for months.
Why the same BMI can mean a different BMR

The Mifflin-St Jeor equation uses total weight, so it cannot see body composition. The Katch-McArdle equation, which our TDEE calculator uses when body fat is entered, works from lean mass: BMR = 370 + 21.6 x lean mass (kg). Take two people who both weigh 82 kg at 165 cm, so both have a BMI of 30.1.

Same BMI, same weight, and a gap of about 265 kcal/day in estimated BMR because one has more lean mass. The body fat percentages here are hypothetical, and a body fat estimate from a tape measure or a scale carries its own error, so treat the gap as an illustration of direction rather than a precise figure.

items: Using BMI to set calories. BMI classifies weight for height; it does not enter the energy formulas, and two people with the same BMI can have different energy needs.
Picking an optimistic activity factor. Moving from 1.375 to 1.55 raises this example from 2,083 to 2,349 kcal/day, an overestimate of about 266 kcal/day if the lower factor is the honest one.
Treating TDEE as exact. It is a formula estimate. Real maintenance can differ, so use your own weight trend over several weeks to adjust.
Never recalculating. As the second table shows, estimates shift by roughly 10 kcal/day for each kilogram of weight change in the BMR part alone.
Chasing a BMI cutoff as the goal. BMI is a screening tool, so combine it with waist size and how you feel.

sections.text: These are estimates, not medical advice. BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Very low calorie intakes should only be followed under medical supervision. If you have a medical condition, are pregnant, take medication, or are under 18 or over 65, talk to a clinician or registered dietitian before changing your eating or exercise.

items: Check BMI and the weight range for your height, as a starting reference only.
Estimate BMR with a calculator and note which equation it used.
Choose an activity factor you would defend honestly, then read TDEE as a maintenance estimate.
Decide any change in calories with a professional, using the TDEE figure as the baseline.
Weigh yourself consistently, watch the trend, and recalculate when your weight has moved.
